sections_menu.h2: What does a complete AI-use disclosure statement look like?

h3.h3: What elements make a disclosure statement complete?

evidence.gloss: Academic disclosure practice: statement must name the tool, its purpose, and oversight extent
evidence.verbatim: Adjacent disclosure practice from academic and research contexts (a different domain, but the same underlying disclosure mechanics) specifies what a disclosure statement needs to capture once that mechanism is chosen: the name of the AI tool used, the purpose it was used for, and the extent of the candidate's own oversight over the output[9].

evidence.gloss: A single consistent disclosure structure simplifies expectations for both discloser and reviewer
evidence.verbatim: A parallel framework built for the same problem argues that a single, consistent disclosure structure simplifies what's expected of the person disclosing and what the reviewer has to check for, rather than leaving both sides to guess at ad hoc phrasing each time[10].

evidence.gloss: Required element: tool identity
evidence.verbatim: the tool name, developer, and version or release date

evidence.gloss: Required element: task performed
evidence.verbatim: the specific task the AI performed (e.g., debugging, boilerplate generation, code review)

evidence.gloss: Required element: extent of use
evidence.verbatim: the extent of use, ranging from a single check to substantial drafting

evidence.gloss: Required element: human verification statement
evidence.verbatim: a statement that a human verified the output before submission[15]

evidence.gloss: Missing elements is top reason disclosures get rejected in academia
evidence.verbatim: Missing any of these elements is cited as the most common reason disclosure statements get sent back for revision in academic settings, which suggests a hackathon disclosure form should force each field rather than accept free text[15].

evidence.gloss: Publishing's AI-disclosure convention defines complete disclosure as three named elements
evidence.verbatim: Outside the hackathon context, the format that AI disclosure statements converge on in publishing is instructive for what "complete disclosure" looks like as a scorable unit: name the tool, describe the reason it was used, and confirm the human reviewed and edited the output

evidence.gloss: Standard publishing AI-disclosure statement template wording
evidence.verbatim: "the author(s) used [NAME OF TOOL / SERVICE] in order to [REASON]. After using this tool/service, the author(s) reviewed and edited the content as needed and take(s) full responsibility"[9]

evidence.gloss: A rubric scores against the three disclosure elements; missing one is incomplete, not automatic non-disclosure
evidence.verbatim: A rubric can score against exactly these three elements — tool named, use-case specified, human review confirmed — and a statement missing any one of them scores as incomplete disclosure rather than automatic non-disclosure.

evidence.gloss: Vague/incomplete disclosure is a leading reason manuscripts get returned during editorial checks
evidence.verbatim: Vague or incomplete disclosure is flagged as "one of the most common reasons manuscripts are returned during editorial checks" in the publishing-disclosure literature[15]

evidence.gloss: A vague disclosure like 'used AI to help' should score lower than an itemized one
evidence.verbatim: the same failure mode applies to hackathon submissions: a candidate who writes "used AI to help" without naming the tool or the task should score lower on the disclosure line item than one who itemizes exactly where AI entered the build.

h3.h3: The AID framework: a model borrowed from academic publishing

evidence.gloss: Academic-publishing disclosure template a hackathon policy could mirror
evidence.verbatim: Disclosure format itself has an established template from academic publishing that a hackathon policy could mirror at the submission level: a named tool, the specific task it was used for, and a statement that output was checked.

evidence.gloss: Practical fix is a defined candidate-disclosure pattern as an explicit policy component, not prohibition alone
evidence.verbatim: the practical fix being a defined candidate-disclosure pattern as one explicit component of the policy, rather than relying on prohibition alone[5]

evidence.gloss: AID framework as the model for candidate disclosure
evidence.verbatim: A workable model for candidate AI disclosure borrows from the academic AI Disclosure (AID) framework, which several journals and universities already use to standardize how contributors report generative AI use.

evidence.gloss: Disclosure statement length and scope
evidence.verbatim: A complete disclosure statement is brief, typically 2 to 4 sentences, and covers the same core elements regardless of the specific tool or task

evidence.gloss: AID structural insight: disclosure appended like acknowledgments, by point of engagement
evidence.verbatim: The AID Framework's structural insight adapts directly to a hackathon submission: the disclosure statement is appended to the end of the work product, similar to an acknowledgments section, and it details each AI tool used and the manner of use based on the distinct points of engagement across the build process[10].

h3.h3: Where should the disclosure live in a submission?

evidence.gloss: Academic publishers' standard disclosure placements
evidence.verbatim: Academic publishers place disclosure in one of several standard locations: the methods section when AI shaped data handling or core logic, a dedicated "AI use" or declaration section, or a note appended just before references[15].

evidence.gloss: Hackathon analogue placement: mandatory submission-form field, not buried in ToS
evidence.verbatim: The closest hackathon analogue is a dedicated, mandatory field in the submission form itself, submitted alongside the code and write-up rather than buried in terms-of-service language the candidate may not read closely.

h3.h3: Matching disclosure depth to how much AI shaped the work

evidence.gloss: Disclosure example: ChatGPT used to draft exploratory data-analysis code
evidence.verbatim: ChatGPT (GPT-5, OpenAI) was used to draft exploratory data-analysis code. All output was tested and verified by the authors before use,

evidence.gloss: Disclosure example: Paperpal used to check grammar/clarity, no new content generated
evidence.verbatim: Paperpal was used to check grammar and clarity in this manuscript. No new content was generated, and all edits were reviewed by the author,

evidence.gloss: Academic engagement categories map to hackathon build categories
evidence.verbatim: In an academic paper, those points of engagement are categories like Conceptualization, Writing—Review & Editing, and Project Administration; a hiring hackathon submission form can substitute build-relevant categories such as scaffolding/boilerplate, debugging, code review, and documentation.

evidence.gloss: AID example names a distinct tool per category rather than one blanket line
evidence.verbatim: An example AID statement built this way names the tool for each category separately rather than issuing one blanket line, e.g., distinguishing which tool assisted "Conceptualization" versus which tool was used for "Writing—Review & Editing"[10].

evidence.gloss: Category-by-category disclosure maps onto the judging rubric
evidence.verbatim: This structure directly serves the judging rubric this article defines: because each category maps to a distinct part of the rubric (architecture decisions vs. code quality vs. write-up), a category-by-category disclosure lets judges see exactly where AI touched the work, rather than getting a single undifferentiated "AI was used" checkbox.

evidence.gloss: Disclosure depth should scale with how much AI shaped the work
evidence.verbatim: Disclosure expectations should scale with how much the AI shaped the actual work, not just whether it was touched.

evidence.gloss: Editing-only use warrants lighter disclosure than core-logic use
evidence.verbatim: Editing- and language-polish-only use (grammar, clarity, formatting) warrants a lighter disclosure than use that shaped the core logic, analysis, or architecture, since the risk to evaluating the candidate's own skill differs sharply between the two[15].

evidence.gloss: Example confirming line for editing/polishing tool disclosure
evidence.verbatim: editing/polishing tools get a short confirming line ("No new content was generated, and all edits were reviewed by the author")

evidence.gloss: Example required statement for coding/debugging tool disclosure
evidence.verbatim: coding/debugging tools with the AI performing "script writing, debugging, chart or figure generation" require a statement that "all code was tested and the resulting figures verified against the source data"[15]

evidence.gloss: Mapping task-type disclosure split onto hiring hackathon depth requirements
evidence.verbatim: For a hiring hackathon, this maps to requiring deeper disclosure (which functions, which files, which logic) when AI assisted with the graded engineering work itself, versus a lighter note when it only helped with the write-up's prose.

sections_menu.h2: How do you actually detect undisclosed AI use in candidate work?

h3.h3: Why the live discussion is the real verification step

evidence.gloss: Because AI can produce polished work, the follow-up conversation is what verifies real understanding
evidence.verbatim: The operating assumption is that AI can produce seemingly polished work across many scenarios, which is precisely why the follow-up discussion with the candidate becomes essential; a conversation is what verifies the candidate actually understands the work behind their submission, rather than having merely turned in an AI-produced artifact[17].

evidence.gloss: Scoring implication: the live discussion/defense is the mechanism that catches undisclosed AI use
evidence.verbatim: This has a direct implication for scoring design: where a hackathon submission is paired with a live discussion or defense (see the judging rubric), that discussion is the mechanism that catches undisclosed or misrepresented AI use, not a separate compliance check bolted onto the policy.

evidence.verbatim: Depending on the role and where the organization sits on the AI-adoption spectrum, it can be valuable to deliberately allow AI use during the hackathon and observe how a candidate uses it, provided the candidate's own expertise remains evident in the outcome[17].

evidence.verbatim: When AI use is built in this way, as an explicit on-the-job competency being evaluated rather than an incidental allowance, the policy needs to set clear parameters and be specific about what is expected, rather than leaving candidates to guess where the boundary sits[17].

evidence.verbatim: In written and submitted materials, flagged patterns include repeated words or phrases, a lack of personalization (generic content that doesn't address the specific task), formatting inconsistencies, different tones or writing styles within a single submission or across a candidate's materials, overly complex or verbose language relative to the task, and similarities between multiple candidates' submitted materials[1].

evidence.gloss: Written-material tell: formatting inconsistencies
evidence.verbatim: formatting inconsistencies

evidence.gloss: Written-material tell: different tones or writing styles within/across a candidate's materials
evidence.verbatim: different tones or writing styles within a single submission or across a candidate's materials

evidence.gloss: Written-material tell: overly complex or verbose language relative to the task
evidence.verbatim: overly complex or verbose language relative to the task

evidence.gloss: Written-material tell: similarities between multiple candidates' submissions
evidence.verbatim: similarities between multiple candidates' submitted materials[1]

evidence.gloss: Detection framework flags rubric-gaming answers (STAR/Big-O/CAP-theorem) as an AI-assistance signature
evidence.verbatim: At the level of technical content specifically, one detection framework flags answers that are "structured to score maximally" against known rubrics — STAR-format behavioral answers, Big-O complexity analysis volunteered on algorithmic questions, or CAP-theorem citations dropped into distributed-systems answers — as a signature of AI-assisted rather than organically reasoned responses[18].

evidence.verbatim: human-authored solutions typically show incremental problem decomposition — breaking a problem down, testing assumptions, hitting dead ends, backtracking

evidence.verbatim: AI-generated solutions "appear fully formed" without that visible process[18]

evidence.verbatim: evidence that detectably AI-authored submissions can be penalized in judging even independent of a formal disclosure violation

sections_menu.h2: How should assessments score AI use instead of just detecting it?

h3.h3: Vendors are shifting to scoring how AI is used, not whether it's used

evidence.gloss: AI-era assessment vendors turned the boilerplate-vs-feature distinction into a scoring philosophy
evidence.verbatim: Coding-assessment vendors building explicitly for the AI era have operationalized this same distinction into a scoring philosophy.

evidence.gloss: One vendor scores approach, AI collaboration, and validation rather than raw output
evidence.verbatim: how candidates approach the problem, how they collaborate with AI, and how they validate and refine solutions,

evidence.gloss: Vendor's premise: question isn't whether AI is used, but whether it's used well
evidence.verbatim: the question is no longer whether a candidate uses AI, but whether they use it well

evidence.gloss: Specific, concrete prompting produces usable output; vague prompts produce a tutorial, not production code
evidence.verbatim: giving the AI specific, concrete context produces usable output, while a vague prompt produces "a tutorial" instead of production-ready code

evidence.gloss: First-person account's top lesson: always verify AI output
evidence.verbatim: always verify AI output

evidence.gloss: AI-generated scaffolding framed as legitimate starting point, not a violation
evidence.verbatim: the AI provides the scaffold, the human provides the judgment,

evidence.verbatim: 500 lines of imperfect, working code beats zero lines of perfect, imaginary code

evidence.verbatim: The competitive differentiator in that framing is not who avoided AI, but who wrote better specifications, made better architectural calls, and debugged more effectively on top of AI-generated output[14].

h3.h3: Rubrics need anchored score bands and evidence to resist gaming

evidence.gloss: Disclosure process credibility depends on a judge-calibration check
evidence.verbatim: A candidate disclosure process is only as credible as the calibration step that checks judges aren't quietly re-introducing the penalty the policy claims not to apply.

evidence.gloss: Rubric design borrows from AI-interview behavioral-anchor scoring and hackathon anti-gaming principles
evidence.verbatim: A rubric that scores disclosed AI use fairly, rather than treating "used AI" as a single pass/fail flag, borrows its structure from two adjacent practices: behavioral-anchor scoring already used in AI-assisted interview evaluation, and the anti-gaming design principles used in hackathon rubrics generally.

evidence.gloss: Anchored score bands plus required evidence are what stop a rubric from being gamed
evidence.verbatim: A hackathon scoring rubric resists gaming only when "every criterion has anchored score bands and a required evidence" component[22].

evidence.gloss: Score the behavior around AI use with named bands, not a yes/no checkbox
evidence.verbatim: Applied to AI use, this means the rubric should not ask judges to simply mark "AI used: yes/no" — it should score the *behavior* candidates demonstrate around AI, the same way competency rubrics score behavior generally: named scoring bands with observable behavior descriptions

evidence.gloss: Example per-line-item AI-use scoring criteria instead of one holistic score
evidence.verbatim: In practice this looks like per-line-item scoring — "prompting and iteration shown," "output verified/debugged by candidate," "disclosure complete and specific" — each mapped to a band, rather than one holistic "AI usage" score.

evidence.gloss: Evidence-based rubrics replace abstract criteria; a criterion too vague to score from artefacts is too vague to keep
evidence.verbatim: Evidence-based hackathon rubrics generally replace abstract criteria with observable evidence: "if a criterion cannot be explained in one sentence and scored from artefacts, it is too vague to improve winner quality"[22].

evidence.gloss: For AI use, the scorable artefact is the disclosure statement plus any process trace submitted
evidence.verbatim: For AI-use specifically, the artefact is the disclosure statement plus whatever trace of process the candidate submits (prompt log, git history, verbal walkthrough of what they built versus what the model generated).

h3.h3: Fixing judges who penalize disclosed AI use

evidence.gloss: Unanchored judge down-scoring of any disclosed AI use risks penalizing transparency over skill
evidence.verbatim: For a hiring hackathon, this means a rubric that lets judges freely down-score any submission that discloses AI use, without anchored criteria, risks penalizing transparency rather than measuring skill — directly undermining the incentive to disclose at all.

evidence.gloss: Fix: score disclosed behavior against specific bands, not a judge's general reaction to AI involvement
evidence.verbatim: The fix mirrors the anchored-evidence approach used elsewhere: score the disclosed behavior against specific bands (verification shown, ownership demonstrated, complete disclosure format) rather than letting a judge's general reaction to "AI was involved" move the score.

evidence.gloss: Human-in-the-Loop-O-Meter: trust-based framework replacing yes/no AI declarations
evidence.verbatim: One proposed structural fix from outside the hackathon context is worth noting as a caveat on binary disclosure models generally: a "trust-based disclosure framework" (the Human-in-the-Loop-O-Meter) that "replaces yes/no AI declarations with a structured way to demonstrate what the human actually contributed"[25]

evidence.gloss: A graduated, evidence-scored disclosure line item outperforms a single AI-use checkbox for fairness and gameability
evidence.verbatim: reinforcing that a graduated, evidence-scored disclosure line item outperforms a single AI-use checkbox for both fairness and gameability.

evidence.gloss: Each AI-use score should trace to the specific evidence that produced it
evidence.verbatim: Whatever point structure the rubric uses, each AI-use score should be traceable to the specific evidence that produced it, consistent with the broader rubric principle that "every score traces to a rubric line and the sentence in the entry that earned it"[26]

evidence.gloss: Per-question scoring should reference the candidate quote that drove it, reviewable side by side
evidence.verbatim: per-question scoring should reference "the candidate quote that drove it," reviewable side by side[23].

sections_menu.h2: How do companies actually enforce their AI-use policies?

evidence.gloss: A defensible rubric-and-disclosure system needs a stated spectrum position and real consequence
evidence.verbatim: a rubric-and-disclosure system only functions as a defensible signal if the policy states which end of that spectrum applies and what the actual consequence is for violating it, rather than leaving it as an unenforced expectation

h3.h3: Attestation vs. disclosure: the two enforcement mechanisms

evidence.gloss: Two enforcement mechanisms named: attestation of no use, or disclosure of use
evidence.verbatim: guidance names two distinct mechanisms — requiring candidates to attest that they used no AI at any stage, or requiring them to disclose what AI they used[1]

evidence.gloss: Attestation-only is a prohibition tier by honor system; disclosure makes extent of use the scored variable
evidence.verbatim: These are not the same policy. An attestation-only tier is effectively a prohibition tier with an honor-system check; a disclosure tier assumes some AI use is expected and instead makes the use itself, and its extent, the scored variable.

evidence.gloss: Compliance across policies turns on disclosure, not on whether AI was used at all
evidence.verbatim: Policies collected from live hiring processes converge on a narrow band of AI assistance that is treated as compliant, and in every case compliance turns on disclosure, not on whether AI touched the work at all.

h3.h3: Strict-end policies: outright bans on AI use

evidence.gloss: Strict-end policy: candidates must affirm they completed assessments independently, without AI
evidence.verbatim: independently and without the assistance of others, or any artificial intelligence or other resources,

evidence.gloss: Strict-end consequence: dishonest candidates (including AI use) withdrawn, further action possible
evidence.verbatim: candidates found to have acted dishonestly, including through AI use, are withdrawn from the process, with further action possible[17]

evidence.gloss: Another company bans AI entirely during application/interview; disqualifies or terminates violators
evidence.verbatim: A separate account describes a company that requires candidates to agree not to use AI during any part of the application or interview process at all, with a policy of disqualifying candidates caught during candidacy and terminating employees discovered to have violated it after hiring[2].

h3.h3: Soft-end policies: expectations without teeth

evidence.gloss: Soft-end policy: candidates asked to use their own words without online aids
evidence.verbatim: use your own words to describe your thoughts and ideas, without use of online aids

evidence.gloss: Soft-end policy is phrased as an expectation, not an enforceable prohibition, with no stated consequence or AI named directly
evidence.verbatim: as an expectation rather than an enforceable prohibition, with no stated consequence

sections_menu.h2: What legal and regulatory requirements apply to AI use in hiring?

h3.h3: What does existing law require for AI-in-hiring disclosure?

evidence.gloss: Existing law already treats AI-in-hiring disclosure as a baseline obligation
evidence.verbatim: Existing law already treats AI-in-hiring disclosure as a baseline obligation, which gives a hackathon organizer a template to work from.

evidence.gloss: Illinois' AI Video Interview Act (2020) requires employer AI disclosure; analysts say it implies candidates could be required to do the same
evidence.verbatim: Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act (2020) requires employers to disclose their own use of AI in the hiring process, a structure that legal analysts note "suggests that employers could require candidates do the same" in reverse[1].

evidence.gloss: Employers drafting candidate AI-disclosure policy advised to follow the "Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights" to avoid disproportionate burden on applicant groups
evidence.verbatim: Any employer restricting or requiring disclosure of a candidate's AI use has been advised to draft that policy with the Biden administration's "Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights" in mind, specifically ensuring the rule doesn't inadvertently or disproportionately burden particular groups of applicants[1].

evidence.gloss: A hackathon's judging process, where AI-assisted work feeds a scored comparative evaluation, sits inside the same transparency expectation even though it isn't a screening algorithm
evidence.verbatim: A hackathon's judging process — where AI-assisted work directly feeds a scored, comparative evaluation of candidates — sits squarely inside that same transparency expectation, even though the hackathon itself is not a screening algorithm.

h3.h3: Which regulations classify hiring AI as high-risk?

evidence.gloss: EU AI Act classifies recruitment/selection/candidate-evaluation AI as "high-risk"; enforcement from Aug 2, 2026; fines up to €35M or 7% of global revenue
evidence.verbatim: the EU AI Act classifies AI systems used in recruitment, selection, and candidate evaluation as "high-risk" with enforcement beginning August 2, 2026 and fines up to €35 million or 7% of global revenue for non-compliance

evidence.gloss: Colorado SB 24-205 (effective June 30, 2026) carries a similar AI oversight mandate
evidence.verbatim: Colorado SB 24-205 (effective June 30, 2026) carries a similar oversight mandate[3]

evidence.gloss: EU AI Act (effective August 2026) classifies employment-decision AI as high-risk, requiring documentation and decision logging
evidence.verbatim: the EU AI Act (full effect August 2026) classifies employment-decision AI as high-risk and requires technical documentation and decision logging[27]

evidence.gloss: NYC Local Law 144 requires independent bias audits and candidate notification
evidence.verbatim: NYC Local Law 144 requires independent bias audits and candidate notification[27].

h3.h3: Why do explainable, auditable scores matter for compliance?

evidence.gloss: AI-hiring regulation increasingly requires explainable, per-candidate score breakdowns
evidence.verbatim: This matters beyond fairness to candidates: AI-hiring regulation increasingly requires explainable, per-candidate score breakdowns

evidence.gloss: An auditable AI-use scoring trail gives hiring teams regulatory defensibility for that part of the rubric
evidence.verbatim: An auditable AI-use scoring trail — which line item, which evidence, which band — gives a hiring team the same defensibility for the AI-use portion of the rubric that the regulation increasingly expects for the screening process as a whole[3][27].
